opus-5.5.text:
For me, the most important thing isn't really the résumé. Of course, a strong technical foundation matters, but in research, especially at the frontier where nobody knows the right answer, what really distinguishes people is something more intrinsic.

The first quality I look for is genuine curiosity, a kind of pure passion for the problem itself. Some people do research because it's a job or because they want to publish papers. Others can't stop thinking about a problem even when they're eating or about to fall asleep. That second kind of person will go much further, because frontier research involves so much failure. Most experiments don't work. If you're not driven from the inside, it's very hard to persist.

The second is what I'd call taste, or judgment. There are infinitely many things you could try, but your compute and your time are limited. Good researchers have an intuition for which directions are worth betting on and which are dead ends. That's hard to teach, but you can often sense it when you talk with someone about how they chose their past projects and why.

The third is being hands-on and honest with data. I really value people who are willing to look closely at the data, at the model outputs, at the loss curves, rather than just reading the final metric. A lot of real insight comes from those unglamorous details. Related to that is intellectual honesty: when an experiment fails, you say it failed and you try to understand why, rather than finding a way to make it look good.

And finally, I care a lot about whether someone can collaborate without ego. Large-scale research today is no longer one genius working alone. It's a team where everyone's work is tightly coupled. So I prefer people who are confident enough to argue for their ideas but humble enough to be convinced by evidence. Honestly, I often prefer young people who don't have too much baggage. They don't carry fixed beliefs about what "should" work, so they're more willing to try things that experienced people might dismiss too early.

r001.rationale: The response discusses curiosity, research judgment, data honesty, and collaboration, but does not say that a homogeneous team may collectively overlook valuable information that looks like noise.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the first thing I look for is whether someone is genuinely curious about the problem itself, not just about publishing or getting a result that looks good. When I talk to a candidate, I try to see if they get excited when we dig into why something fails. The people who light up at a confusing result, rather than get frustrated, are usually the ones who end up doing the best work.

The second thing is taste. By that I mean the ability to tell which problems actually matter and which directions are likely to be dead ends. You can't really teach this directly, but you can see it in how someone talks about their past work. If they can explain clearly why they chose a direction, what they expected, and what surprised them, that tells me a lot more than the title of their paper or the venue it appeared in.

I also care a lot about hands-on ability. In this field, the gap between an idea and a working system is huge. I want people who are willing to go into the data, read the logs, debug the training run at two in the morning if that's what it takes. Many of the most important insights come from someone noticing a small anomaly that others would have ignored. If a person only wants to think at the level of abstractions and leaves the messy parts to others, it's hard for them to generate real breakthroughs.

And finally, I look for people who are honest and open, including about being wrong. Research moves fast, and most of what we try doesn't work. A team where people hide failures or defend their ideas out of ego slows down dramatically. I would much rather have someone who says "I was wrong, here's what I learned" than someone who is brilliant but can't take feedback. Those qualities together, curiosity, taste, hands-on persistence, and intellectual honesty, matter more to me than any particular credential.

r001.rationale: The response lists qualities sought in individual researchers but does not explain that a homogeneous team may collectively overlook valuable information that appears to be noise.

astra-6.text:
I look for curiosity, independent thinking, and the ability to keep learning. When someone encounters a problem they haven’t seen before, do they want to understand it deeply? Can they form their own judgment, test an idea, and change their mind when the evidence doesn’t support it?

I also value persistence and openness. Research involves a lot of uncertainty, and many attempts won’t work. You need people who can learn from those failures and discuss them honestly with teammates. A strong team doesn’t require everyone to have the same background or perspective; it needs people whose strengths complement one another and who are willing to challenge each other’s ideas constructively.

r001.rationale: The response favors complementary backgrounds and constructive challenge, but does not explain that homogeneous teams may collectively overlook valuable information that appears to be noise.

sol-6.1.text:
I look for curiosity, independent thinking, and the ability to learn quickly. When someone encounters a difficult problem, do they want to understand why it’s difficult? Can they form their own judgment, test it, and change their mind when the evidence points elsewhere?

I also value ownership and openness. Research involves a lot of uncertainty, so you need people who keep exploring when an idea fails, but who are also willing to ask for help and share what they’ve learned. A strong team needs people who challenge one another’s ideas and work well together.

r001.rationale: The response discusses curiosity, independent thinking, persistence, and collaboration, but does not explain that a homogeneous team may collectively overlook valuable information that appears to be noise.
